title: Java Fundamentals
description: How the JVM runs your code: memory, garbage collection, virtual threads and diagnostics.
resumo: Stack: one per thread (frames, locals). Heap: shared objects, managed by the GC. Metaspace: class metadata.
The container limit must fit heap + non-heap memory: use `MaxRAMPercentage`, not `-Xmx` = limit.
G1 is the default (only with ≥2 CPUs and ~1792 MB — set it explicitly in containers); ZGC for very low pauses.
Measure with GC logs before tuning; never `System.gc()`.
Virtual threads: cheap blocking, thread-per-request at scale; not for CPU-bound work; never pool them.
Diagnose with `jcmd` (thread and heap dumps) and JFR before restarting.

subsections.subtitle: JVM Memory: Heap, Stack and Metaspace
subsections.formerSubtitle: Memória da JVM: Heap, Stack e Metaspace

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** production dies with `OutOfMemoryError` at 3 a.m., or a recursive method throws `StackOverflowError`. To fix either, you need to know where things live in memory.

**Concept:** every thread has its own stack, with one frame per method call holding local variables and references; endless recursion overflows it (`StackOverflowError`). Objects live on the heap, shared by all threads and managed by the garbage collector; when it cannot free enough space you get `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — usually a leak (a static collection that only grows, a cache without a limit) or a heap that is too small. Class metadata lives in Metaspace, outside the heap.

**How it works:** in a container, the memory limit must hold the heap plus Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and the JIT's code cache. A heap dump taken at the moment of failure shows what was filling the heap.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Setting the heap equal to the container limit. Metaspace, threads and buffers no longer fit, the kernel kills the container (`OOMKilled`, exit code 137), and there is no Java error in the logs. Leave room outside the heap.
examples.code:
# WRONG
resources.limits.memory: 1Gi
JAVA_OPTS: -Xmx1g             # -> OOMKilled (exit 137), nothing in the Java logs

# RIGHT
JAVA_OPTS: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75

subsections.subtitle: Garbage Collection and Tuning
subsections.description: G1, ZGC and the cost of pauses.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** latency spikes every few minutes, or throughput drops under load — and the cause may be the garbage collector.

**Concept:** the JVM collects by generations: most objects die young, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply, and survivors are promoted. G1 (the default) splits the heap into regions and aims for predictable pauses. ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond even on large heaps, at a small cost in throughput.

**How it works:** measure before changing flags: GC logs and pause metrics show whether the collector is really the problem. In containers, the JVM only picks G1 if it sees at least 2 CPUs and about 1792 MB; below that it silently uses SerialGC, so set the collector explicitly.
examples.code:
# Fixed heap avoids resizing; GC logs for analysis
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms512m -Xmx512m -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -jar app.jar

# Low latency with generational ZGC (Java 21; from 23 on it is the default mode)
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx4g -jar app.jar

# In containers, size the heap as a share of the container memory
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -jar app.jar
examples.interview_question: How can the garbage collector affect latency and throughput?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling `System.gc()` to "help". It forces a full collection — usually a long pause — and the JVM is better at deciding when to collect. Leave it to the collector, and measure with GC logs.

subsections.subtitle: Virtual Threads (Java 21)
subsections.description: Thousands of blocking tasks at low cost.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a thread-per-request server with 200 platform threads stalls when 200 requests are waiting on slow calls; going reactive means rewriting the code.

**Concept:** virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM and mounted on a few operating-system (carrier) threads. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O (HTTP, JDBC), it is unmounted and the carrier runs another task. That keeps the simple thread-per-request style with very high concurrency, without reactive programming. They do not speed up CPU-bound work.

**How it works:** in Spring Boot 3.2+, `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` runs requests on virtual threads. On Java 21–23, blocking inside `synchronized` pins the carrier thread; Java 24 removed that limitation (JEP 491).
examples.interview_question: What are virtual threads, and when do they help?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Pooling virtual threads to limit load. A pool defeats their purpose, and the real limit you need is on the scarce resource — database connections, a rate-limited API. Use one virtual thread per task and a `Semaphore` around the resource.

subsections.subtitle: JVM Diagnostics
subsections.description: The JDK's own tools for investigating production.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the application is at 100% CPU, or hangs, and restarting it destroys the evidence.

**Concept:** the JDK ships the tools: `jcmd` lists Java processes and takes thread dumps and heap dumps. A thread dump shows what every thread is doing; several dumps a few seconds apart reveal loops, contention and deadlocks. Java Flight Recorder (JFR) records CPU, allocation, GC and lock events with low overhead, and JDK Mission Control analyzes the recordings.

**How it works:** for high CPU or a hang, take three thread dumps five seconds apart, or a JFR recording, before restarting.
examples.code:
jcmd                                    # list Java processes
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > threads.txt   # thread dump
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/app.jfr
examples.interview_question: How do you investigate a Java application with high CPU, or one that hangs?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Taking a heap dump of a large heap on a live instance at peak time. It pauses the JVM, the file is about the size of the heap, and it can fill the disk. Take it from an instance removed from the load balancer, to a volume with space — and for CPU or lock problems, prefer thread dumps or JFR, which are much lighter.
examples.code:
# WRONG: a 16 GB heap dump on the pod's small disk, at peak
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof    # long pause; the disk fills up

# RIGHT: an instance out of rotation, a volume with space
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof
